1. Intuition and a numerical example

A household with a monthly income of €2,000 chooses a basket. Suppose every price and its income double. A basket xxx was affordable before if p⋅x≤2000p\cdot x\le 2000p⋅x≤2000⁠; it is affordable now if 2p⋅x≤40002p\cdot x\le 40002p⋅x≤4000⁠, which is the same inequality. The budget set has not moved, so a household that cares about quantities, not about nominal values, has no reason to change its basket. Demand is *homogeneous of degree zero* in prices and income: this is the formal definition of "no money illusion". The econometrician observes JJJ prices and income YYY and writes the demand for good 1 as
log⁡q1=β0+∑j=1Jβjlog⁡pj+βJ+1log⁡Y+u.(1)\log q_1=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\beta_j\log p_j+\beta_{J+1}\log Y+u . \qquad \htmlId{equation-1}{(1)}logq1​=β0​+j=1∑J​βj​logpj​+βJ+1​logY+u.(1)
Section 3 shows that multiplying all prices and income by λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 multiplies q1q_1q1​ by λθ\lambda^{\theta}λθ⁠, where θ≡∑j=1Jβj+βJ+1\theta\equiv\sum_{j=1}^J\beta_j+\beta_{J+1}θ≡∑j=1J​βj​+βJ+1​⁠. With θ=0.1\theta=0.1θ=0.1⁠, doubling prices and income raises demand by 20.1−1=7.2%2^{0.1}-1=7.2\%20.1−1=7.2%⁠, although nothing real has changed: that is money illusion. Homogeneity is the restriction θ=0\theta=0θ=0⁠.

2. From the utility function to the demand function

**The general result.** The Marshallian demand x(p,Y)x(p,Y)x(p,Y) maximises U(x)U(x)U(x) over the budget set B(p,Y)={x≥0: p⋅x≤Y}B(p,Y)=\{x\ge0:\ p\cdot x\le Y\}B(p,Y)={x≥0: p⋅x≤Y}⁠. (I write UUU for utility and keep uuu for the error term.) For any λ>0\lambda>0λ>0⁠:
B(λp,λY)={x≥0: (λp)⋅x≤λY}={x≥0: λ (p⋅x)≤λY}={x≥0: p⋅x≤Y}(divide by λ>0)=B(p,Y),x(λp,λY)=arg⁡max⁡x∈B(λp,λY)U(x)=arg⁡max⁡x∈B(p,Y)U(x)=x(p,Y).(2)\begin{aligned} B(\lambda p,\lambda Y)&=\{x\ge0:\ (\lambda p)\cdot x\le \lambda Y\} \\ &=\{x\ge0:\ \lambda\,(p\cdot x)\le \lambda Y\} \\ &=\{x\ge0:\ p\cdot x\le Y\}\qquad\text{(divide by }\lambda>0) \\ &=B(p,Y), \\ x(\lambda p,\lambda Y)&=\arg\max_{x\in B(\lambda p,\lambda Y)}U(x)=\arg\max_{x\in B(p,Y)}U(x)=x(p,Y). && \htmlId{equation-2}{(2)} \end{aligned}B(λp,λY)x(λp,λY)​={x≥0: (λp)⋅x≤λY}={x≥0: λ(p⋅x)≤λY}={x≥0: p⋅x≤Y}(divide by λ>0)=B(p,Y),=argx∈B(λp,λY)max​U(x)=argx∈B(p,Y)max​U(x)=x(p,Y).​​(2)​
Homogeneity is therefore a consequence of the budget constraint, not an assumption about the shape of preferences. It requires only that UUU depends on quantities and not on nominal magnitudes, and that the maximiser is unique (otherwise the demand *set* is homogeneous). **Cobb–Douglas.** Let U(x)=∑jαjlog⁡xjU(x)=\sum_j\alpha_j\log x_jU(x)=∑j​αj​logxj​ with αj>0\alpha_j>0αj​>0 and ∑jαj=1\sum_j\alpha_j=1∑j​αj​=1⁠. The budget constraint binds because UUU is increasing.

Comparing (8) with (1): β0=log⁡α1\beta_0=\log\alpha_1β0​=logα1​⁠, β1=−1\beta_1=-1β1​=−1⁠, βj=0\beta_j=0βj​=0 for j=2,…,Jj=2,\dots,Jj=2,…,J⁠, βJ+1=1\beta_{J+1}=1βJ+1​=1⁠, so θ=−1+0+1=0\theta=-1+0+1=0θ=−1+0+1=0⁠. Directly on (7):

**Stone–Geary (linear expenditure system).** Cobb–Douglas forces zero cross-price elasticities and a unit income elasticity. Let instead U(x)=∑jαjlog⁡(xj−γj)U(x)=\sum_j\alpha_j\log(x_j-\gamma_j)U(x)=∑j​αj​log(xj​−γj​)⁠, with αj>0\alpha_j>0αj​>0⁠, ∑jαj=1\sum_j\alpha_j=1∑j​αj​=1⁠, xj>γjx_j>\gamma_jxj​>γj​ and Y>∑jpjγjY>\sum_jp_j\gamma_jY>∑j​pj​γj​ (Stone, 1954). The Lagrangian is the same as (3) with log⁡(xj−γj)\log(x_j-\gamma_j)log(xj​−γj​) in place of log⁡xj\log x_jlogxj​⁠; the condition ∂L/∂μ=0\partial\mathcal L/\partial\mu=0∂L/∂μ=0 is again (5).

The multiplier is the inverse of *supernumerary* income (11); the household buys the committed quantity γ1\gamma_1γ1​ and spends a share α1\alpha_1α1​ of what is left (12). Homogeneity, directly on (12):
x1(λp,λY)=γ1+α1λp1(λY−∑j=1Jλpjγj)=γ1+λ α1λ p1(Y−∑j=1Jpjγj)=x1(p,Y).\begin{aligned} x_1(\lambda p,\lambda Y)&=\gamma_1+\frac{\alpha_1}{\lambda p_1}\Big(\lambda Y-\sum_{j=1}^J\lambda p_j\gamma_j\Big) =\gamma_1+\frac{\lambda\,\alpha_1}{\lambda\,p_1}\Big(Y-\sum_{j=1}^Jp_j\gamma_j\Big)=x_1(p,Y). \end{aligned}x1​(λp,λY)​=γ1​+λp1​α1​​(λY−j=1∑J​λpj​γj​)=γ1​+λp1​λα1​​(Y−j=1∑J​pj​γj​)=x1​(p,Y).​
*Elasticities.* Differentiate (12); for the own price, use (12) in the form (α1/p1)(Y−∑jpjγj)=x1−γ1(\alpha_1/p_1)(Y-\sum_jp_j\gamma_j)=x_1-\gamma_1(α1​/p1​)(Y−∑j​pj​γj​)=x1​−γ1​⁠:
∂x1∂Y=α1p1⟹η1=Yx1∂x1∂Y=α1Yp1x1∂x1∂pj=−α1γjp1 (j≠1)⟹ε1j=pjx1∂x1∂pj=−α1γjpjp1x1∂x1∂p1=−α1p12(Y−∑jpjγj)−α1γ1p1=−x1−γ1+α1γ1p1⟹ε11=−1+(1−α1)γ1x1.(13)\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial Y}=\frac{\alpha_1}{p_1} \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \eta_1=\frac{Y}{x_1}\frac{\partial x_1}{\partial Y}=\frac{\alpha_1Y}{p_1x_1} \\ \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial p_j}=-\frac{\alpha_1\gamma_j}{p_1}\ (j\ne1) \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \varepsilon_{1j}=\frac{p_j}{x_1}\frac{\partial x_1}{\partial p_j}=-\frac{\alpha_1\gamma_jp_j}{p_1x_1} \\ \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial p_1}=-\frac{\alpha_1}{p_1^2}\Big(Y-\sum_{j}p_j\gamma_j\Big)-\frac{\alpha_1\gamma_1}{p_1}=-\frac{x_1-\gamma_1+\alpha_1\gamma_1}{p_1} \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \varepsilon_{11}=-1+\frac{(1-\alpha_1)\gamma_1}{x_1}. && \htmlId{equation-13}{(13)} \end{aligned}∂Y∂x1​​=p1​α1​​∂pj​∂x1​​=−p1​α1​γj​​ (j=1)∂p1​∂x1​​=−p12​α1​​(Y−j∑​pj​γj​)−p1​α1​γ1​​=−p1​x1​−γ1​+α1​γ1​​​⟹η1​=x1​Y​∂Y∂x1​​=p1​x1​α1​Y​⟹ε1j​=x1​pj​​∂pj​∂x1​​=−p1​x1​α1​γj​pj​​⟹ε11​=−1+x1​(1−α1​)γ1​​.​​(13)​

Numerically, with J=3J=3J=3⁠, α=(0.3,0.3,0.4)\alpha=(0.3,0.3,0.4)α=(0.3,0.3,0.4)⁠, γ=(2,3,1)\gamma=(2,3,1)γ=(2,3,1)⁠, p=(2,1,1.5)p=(2,1,1.5)p=(2,1,1.5)⁠, Y=20Y=20Y=20⁠: x1=3.725x_1=3.725x1​=3.725⁠, ε11=−0.624\varepsilon_{11}=-0.624ε11​=−0.624⁠, ε12=−0.121\varepsilon_{12}=-0.121ε12​=−0.121⁠, ε13=−0.060\varepsilon_{13}=-0.060ε13​=−0.060⁠, η1=0.805\eta_1=0.805η1​=0.805⁠; the sum is exactly zero. **Back to model (1): Euler's identity.** The zero sum is not a property of Stone–Geary; it holds for every demand satisfying (2). Fix (p,Y)(p,Y)(p,Y) and let g(λ)=x1(λp,λY)g(\lambda)=x_1(\lambda p,\lambda Y)g(λ)=x1​(λp,λY)⁠.

In (1), ε1j=∂log⁡q1/∂log⁡pj=βj\varepsilon_{1j}=\partial\log q_1/\partial\log p_j=\beta_jε1j​=∂logq1​/∂logpj​=βj​ and η1=βJ+1\eta_1=\beta_{J+1}η1​=βJ+1​ are constant, so (14) reads θ=0\theta=0θ=0⁠. Model (1) is a constant-elasticity approximation to a utility-generated demand, and testing θ=0\theta=0θ=0 tests Euler's identity. The approximation has limits: a double-log demand with unrestricted elasticities is not, in general, exactly and globally derivable from a utility function, since integrability imposes further restrictions (LaFrance, 1986, for incomplete systems of constant-elasticity demands). Homogeneity is the part of the theory that a single equation can carry. **Maintained assumptions.** (i) Scaling by λ\lambdaλ changes neither preferences nor the distribution of uuu⁠: homogeneity concerns E(log⁡q1∣p,Y)E(\log q_1\mid p,Y)E(logq1​∣p,Y)⁠. (ii) Rejecting θ=0\theta=0θ=0 rejects *jointly* the absence of money illusion and the maintained specification (constant elasticities, exogenous prices and income).

3. Imposing the restriction

**The restriction.** Replace every pjp_jpj​ by λpj\lambda p_jλpj​ and YYY by λY\lambda YλY in (1):
log⁡q1(λp,λY)=β0+∑j=1Jβjlog⁡(λpj)+βJ+1log⁡(λY)+u=β0+∑j=1Jβj(log⁡λ+log⁡pj)+βJ+1(log⁡λ+log⁡Y)+u=β0+∑j=1Jβjlog⁡pj+βJ+1log⁡Y+u⏟log⁡q1(p,Y)+(∑j=1Jβj+βJ+1)log⁡λ=log⁡q1(p,Y)+θlog⁡λ.(15)\begin{aligned} \log q_1(\lambda p,\lambda Y)&=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^J\beta_j\log(\lambda p_j)+\beta_{J+1}\log(\lambda Y)+u \\ &=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^J\beta_j(\log\lambda+\log p_j)+\beta_{J+1}(\log\lambda+\log Y)+u \\ &=\underbrace{\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^J\beta_j\log p_j+\beta_{J+1}\log Y+u}_{\log q_1(p,Y)}+\Big(\sum_{j=1}^J\beta_j+\beta_{J+1}\Big)\log\lambda \\ &=\log q_1(p,Y)+\theta\log\lambda. && \htmlId{equation-15}{(15)} \end{aligned}logq1​(λp,λY)​=β0​+j=1∑J​βj​log(λpj​)+βJ+1​log(λY)+u=β0​+j=1∑J​βj​(logλ+logpj​)+βJ+1​(logλ+logY)+u=logq1​(p,Y)β0​+j=1∑J​βj​logpj​+βJ+1​logY+u​​+(j=1∑J​βj​+βJ+1​)logλ=logq1​(p,Y)+θlogλ.​​(15)​
Homogeneity requires θlog⁡λ=0\theta\log\lambda=0θlogλ=0 for all λ>0\lambda>0λ>0⁠. A product of two numbers is zero only if one of them is. Taking λ=2\lambda=2λ=2⁠, so that log⁡λ≠0\log\lambda\ne0logλ=0⁠, shows that θ=0\theta=0θ=0 is necessary; conversely θ=0\theta=0θ=0 makes (15) hold for every λ\lambdaλ⁠. Hence
homogeneity of degree zero⟺∑j=1Jβj+βJ+1=0.(16)\text{homogeneity of degree zero}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sum_{j=1}^J\beta_j+\beta_{J+1}=0. \qquad \htmlId{equation-16}{(16)}homogeneity of degree zero⟺j=1∑J​βj​+βJ+1​=0.(16)
**Solving the restriction.** Any of the J+1J+1J+1 slope coefficients can be eliminated; take the last price elasticity βJ\beta_JβJ​⁠:
∑j=1J−1βj+βJ+βJ+1=0βJ=−(∑j=1J−1βj+βJ+1).(17)\begin{aligned} \sum_{j=1}^{J-1}\beta_j+\beta_J+\beta_{J+1}&=0 \\ \beta_J&=-\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}\beta_j+\beta_{J+1}\Big). && \htmlId{equation-17}{(17)} \end{aligned}j=1∑J−1​βj​+βJ​+βJ+1​βJ​​=0=−(j=1∑J−1​βj​+βJ+1​).​​(17)​
Split the price sum in (1), substitute (17), expand and regroup:
log⁡q1=β0+∑j=1J−1βjlog⁡pj+βJlog⁡pJ+βJ+1log⁡Y+u=β0+∑j=1J−1βjlog⁡pj−(∑j=1J−1βj+βJ+1)log⁡pJ+βJ+1log⁡Y+u=β0+∑j=1J−1βjlog⁡pj−∑j=1J−1βjlog⁡pJ−βJ+1log⁡pJ+βJ+1log⁡Y+u=β0+∑j=1J−1βj (log⁡pj−log⁡pJ)+βJ+1 (log⁡Y−log⁡pJ)+ulog⁡q1=β0+∑j=1J−1βjlog⁡pjpJ+βJ+1log⁡YpJ+u.(18)\begin{aligned} \log q_1&=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}\beta_j\log p_j+\beta_J\log p_J+\beta_{J+1}\log Y+u \\ &=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}\beta_j\log p_j-\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}\beta_j+\beta_{J+1}\Big)\log p_J+\beta_{J+1}\log Y+u \\ &=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}\beta_j\log p_j-\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}\beta_j\log p_J-\beta_{J+1}\log p_J+\beta_{J+1}\log Y+u \\ &=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}\beta_j\,(\log p_j-\log p_J)+\beta_{J+1}\,(\log Y-\log p_J)+u \\ \log q_1&=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}\beta_j\log\frac{p_j}{p_J}+\beta_{J+1}\log\frac{Y}{p_J}+u. && \htmlId{equation-18}{(18)} \end{aligned}logq1​logq1​​=β0​+j=1∑J−1​βj​logpj​+βJ​logpJ​+βJ+1​logY+u=β0​+j=1∑J−1​βj​logpj​−(j=1∑J−1​βj​+βJ+1​)logpJ​+βJ+1​logY+u=β0​+j=1∑J−1​βj​logpj​−j=1∑J−1​βj​logpJ​−βJ+1​logpJ​+βJ+1​logY+u=β0​+j=1∑J−1​βj​(logpj​−logpJ​)+βJ+1​(logY−logpJ​)+u=β0​+j=1∑J−1​βj​logpJ​pj​​+βJ+1​logpJ​Y​+u.​​(18)​
